rules:
===RULES===
1. Output exactly one line: the rewritten instruction itself, and nothing else — no headings, labels, bullet points, quotation marks, reasoning, or notes of any kind (never text like "Thinking Process:"). If unsure what to write, copy the input instruction unchanged rather than output anything else.
2. If the instruction is already a short direct command — it starts with a base-form verb (like "put", "take", "fold"; not "moved", "puts", or "putting") or is a terse caption fragment (like "put pan in sink", "lever vertical to front"), runs under about 15 words, and contains no "please", "kindly", "I", "me", or "you", and no multi-word description standing in for an object's name (colour plus a plain vague noun, like "the orange vegetable" or "the green thing", is a name, not a description) — output it exactly as given: do not add or remove articles, fix spelling or grammar, change capitalisation or punctuation, or swap any word for a synonym. Exception: an instruction whose main verb is transfer, shift, carry, bring, relocate, transport, convey, or deposit is not already in the right form even when short — rewrite it like any other instruction, normally by swapping that verb for "put" or "place" and fitting the goal with "on" or "in" ("Transfer the carrot over to the wheel." → "put the carrot on the wheel"). Second exception: an instruction of the shape "Pick up X and put it on Y" or "Take X and set it down on Y", where no place other than Y is named and the final clause carries no orientation word ("upright", "standing", "vertically", "flat"), collapses to its final clause alone, keeping that clause's exact words and adding nothing ("Pick up the carrot and set it down on the keyboard." → "set the carrot down on the keyboard.").
3. Rewrite the instruction as a short, plain imperative that keeps the same objects and goal.
4. When a multi-word description stands in for an object's name, replace it with the everyday one-word name it identifies ("the handheld implement for lifting food" → "the spatula"); if the description fits several objects, pick the most ordinary kitchen word that fits ("the handled cooking vessel" → "the pot"), never keep the ornate description, but never shorten an object's name past the point where it says what the thing is — a description of a cola can becomes "the coke can" or "the red can", not "the can". Replace a rare or specialist object name with the ordinary everyday word for the same thing — "ramekin" → "bowl", "aubergine" → "eggplant", "crockery" → "dishes" — but never swap between two ordinary names ("plate" never becomes "dish", "cloth" never becomes "towel"). When the instruction already names something in one or two plain everyday words — even vaguely, like "object", "thing", "vegetable", or "robot hand" — keep those exact words and substitute nothing. If you cannot tell what object is meant at all, copy the whole instruction unchanged.
5. Never drop or change a stated colour, size, number, material, or position word, and keep both sides of an "or" choice — "the silver lid on the silver pot" keeps both "silver"s, "the little spoon" keeps "little", "pot or pan" never becomes just "pot". Never add one either: no colour, size, number, or location the instruction does not state. Only politeness, conditions ("if…", "provided that…", "assuming…"), and leftover words of a description you have already replaced may be dropped ("the orange, cone-shaped vegetable" → "the orange carrot": the colour stays, "cone-shaped" goes). A texture or material word attached to a name you replaced is not a leftover — it stays ("the woven textile" → "the woven cloth").
6. Keep the small words of any part that is already plain — "lift the pot up out of the sink" keeps "up", "take the lid off" keeps "off". A verb that is already common — set, lay, grab, drop, rest, slide, stack, leave, and the like — is kept, never swapped for a synonym. When replacing an ornate verb, use the first common one that fits: put, place, take, pick up, move, open, close, fold, unfold. Replace bookish prepositions with everyday ones: "atop" → "on top of", "upon" → "on", "within" → "in", "beneath" → "under"; and drop the wrapper "the surface of" — "onto the surface of the plate" → "on the plate". When rewriting, produce one single command, never the two-part "pick up X and put it on Y": if the instruction names a real starting place, keep it in the form "move X from A to B" ("move the carrot from the table to the plate"); if it names no starting place, or only a vacuous one ("its current location", "where it sits", "its current station"), drop the source and write "put X on Y".
7. When the instruction is about moving the robot's own hand, gripper, or arm itself — nothing being picked up, carried, or placed — rewrite it as the caption "end effector transition from X to Y", reusing the instruction's own words for the start and end points ("Transfer the robot hand from the first piece to the second one." → "end effector transition from the first piece to the second piece"); never write "hand", "gripper", or "arm" for the robot's manipulator, and never reword an instruction that already says "end effector".
8. If the instruction is a plain direct command wrapped only in politeness — "please", "kindly", "Can you … for me?", "Could you …?", "I would like you to …" — output it exactly as given, politeness and all: do not strip the wrapper, and change nothing else. Politeness words are only dropped when the rest of the instruction needs rewriting anyway.

===RATIONALE===
**I found the mechanism behind both regressions, and it changes my read of my own last two books.** I had attributed the iter_03 dip (0.3090) to redraw noise, resubmitted the same restrictions plus one fix, and dipped again (0.3056). Two consecutive dips of the same sign demanded a real mechanism, and the bank supplies one that the 40-pair eval sample could never show: **the narrowing clauses froze inputs whose collapse wins at validation scale.** The iter_03/04 books restricted the collapse to literal "Pick up X and …" openings and froze "Grab X and …"/"Take X and …" — a restriction fit to a single measured loss ('Grab that red aluminum can…' collapse, −16.7 at n=18). But the bank's gt pairs say Take-collapses are large wins in general: 'take the coke can and put it on the plate' holds **30.6 at n=64** against 61.1 at n=286 for the single-command form, and 'take the coke can and place it on the plate' 36.1 vs 52.8 — collapsing a Take-input gains ~25–30 points wherever the bank has measured it. The politeness bar likewise blocked the one strip that measurably wins ('grab that spoon and set it on the cloth', 66.7 at n=18 vs its polite base at 50.0). The eval sample contains exactly one Grab-input and one Take-adjacent polite input; validation evidently contains more, and the broad exception wins on them. So this book **reverts to the best book's broad collapse shapes and unsealed rule 8**, not as a capitulation to the scoreboard but because the bank's own pairs support the broad behavior — the single aluminum-can counterexample is one input, not a family. Lesson recorded for future authors: never restrict a firing rule on the strength of one paired draw when bank-level pairs for the same shape point the other way.

**The two changes kept are the ones whose evidence is multi-draw, bank-confirmed, and unconditional.** (1) The orientation-word exclusion, now inserted into the *broad* exception: 'Pick up the red cola can and place it upright inside the white bowl.' collapsed at −33.3 in **three consecutive draws** under the best book (cumulative 3/18 vs 9/18, on top of the bank pair 55.6 vs 50.0), and froze at exactly 0 the one draw the exclusion was active. Unlike the Grab/Take freeze, this exclusion keys on the modifier ("upright", "standing", "vertically", "flat"), not the opening verb, so it removes only the measured-losing family while leaving every Take/Grab/Pick-up collapse the bank endorses. (2) The surface-wrapper strip in rule 6: the kept wrapper held 16.7 across five draws (n≈48) against 38.9 at n=102 for the bare form, and the live strip has now won +33.3 in two consecutive draws on the same input plus +50 and +33.3 on the towel task. It is a pure rewrite improvement that restricts nothing.

**Everything else is reproduced character for character from the best book**, including rule 8 without the seal sentence — the seal solved a leak (−16.7 once) that the reverted broad exception makes moot, and blocking polite strips outright costs the measured grab-spoon win. Rules 1, 3, 4, 5, 7 are identical across all recent books and their portfolios keep replicating: this round's outcomes ran the standing winners again ('put the cola can down in the bowl' +16.7 — the rare-noun clause's fifth consecutive positive; taproot→wheel +33.3; 'put the red aluminum can on the plate' +33.3; keyboard collapse +33.3, its sixth consecutive draw; 'put the carrot on the plate.' +33.3 — the surface strip's third).

**Standing conflict, resolved explicitly:** the audit's suggestion to restrict atop→"on top of" when the destination carries a modifier now has an n=18 pair behind the loss side ('put the carrot on top of the dining plate' 16.7 vs base 33.3, three draws) — but the conditional replacement ("→ on" for modifier destinations) is still unmeasured, the dining-pair probe has not landed, and the mapping's overall live record remains positive (+33.3/+16.7/0/−16.7 last audit). The mapping stays as-is; changing it on the loss side alone would repeat the exact one-sided-evidence mistake this rationale opens with.

**Probe queue, now five rounds empty — re-listing unchanged, in priority order:** (a) 'put the carrot on top of the dining plate' vs 'put the carrot on the dining plate' at n≥24 (the atop-mapping conditional); (b) 'Transfer the carrot over to the wheel.' vs 'put the carrot on the wheel' at n≥24 (seven eval draws at 0→0; the conveyance exception still has no direct price); (c) 'put the spoon atop the towel' vs 'put the carrot atop the plate' at n≥24 (the 75-vs-33 contradiction); (d) 'take the coke can and set it on the plate' vs 'set the coke can on the plate' at n≥24 — a fresh Take-collapse pair to confirm the mechanism this revision rests on; (e) the or-choice pair at n≥24 (rule 5's or-clause still rests on one n=12 probe after eight draws unexercised).
